strengths: Novel problem formulation: First to explicitly address high-resolution image editing with diffusion models, clearly distinguishing it from standard generation and super-resolution
Sound and well-motivated technical approach: Transfer function learning to inject fine-grained details through diffusion trajectories is intuitive and technically correct
Comprehensive methodology: Systematically addresses practical challenges including detail injection, patch consistency, and content preservation through novel synchronization mechanisms
Strong experimental results: Consistently outperforms diffusion-based SR baselines across multiple metrics (HaarPSI, M-MSE, M-SSIM, M-PSNR) with properly masked variants
Excellent reproducibility: Provides pseudocode (Algorithm 1), detailed mathematical formulations, implementation details using PyTorch, and references to official codebases
Clear presentation with effective visualizations: Figures 1-5 effectively communicate the task and method; qualitative results clearly demonstrate capability
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: Tested exclusively on AI-generated synthetic images with no evaluation on real photographs or natural images, fundamentally limiting claims about real-world applicability

Missing computational cost analysis: No discussion of memory, runtime, or computational complexity; no inference time comparison with baselines despite patch-wise optimization potentially being expensive

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Only compares against diffusion-based SR methods (DiT-SR, DiT4SR, PISA-SR, TSD-SR); missing comparisons with recent instruction-based editing methods, FLUX, and the naive baseline (edit then super-resolve)

Weak perceptual and semantic evaluation: No user studies to validate quality claims; metrics inadequate for measuring semantic correctness of edits; unclear how well fine-grained details are actually preserved on real content
Limited hyperparameter analysis: Only hyperparameter τ is ablated; synchronization strategy components (blended Tweedie weights, resampling) lack justification and sensitivity analysis
Acknowledged limitations unaddressed: Section G admits suboptimal results due to pretrained model constraints and artifacts from low-resolution translation methods but proposes no solutions

Insufficient theoretical justification: Why transfer functions effectively capture fine-grained details remains unclear; no visualization of learned transfers; no explanation for advantage over direct high-resolution training
Dataset limitations: Only 400 image-text pairs; limited to specific edit types; edits generated via ChatGPT without diversity analysis or quality control metrics
Patch synchronization complexity unjustified: Complex mechanism with blended Tweedie updates and resampling lacks ablation against simpler alternatives
Missing failure case analysis: No visual demonstration of failure modes or artifacts despite acknowledged limitations; only shows successful results

strengths: Novel problem formulation introducing high-resolution image editing as a defined task
Comprehensive technical pipeline with well-motivated design (patch-wise optimization, synchronization mechanism, detail enhancement)
Extensive experimental evaluation across 1K and 2K scenarios with multiple metrics and ablation studies
Good visual results demonstrating fine-grained detail preservation and semantic correctness
Detailed methodology with pseudo-code and implementation details supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (diffusion editing, Null-text inversion, patch synchronization) without significant new insights
Misleading problem formulation: title overstates contribution; method still requires high-resolution source conditioning and editing occurs at low-resolution with super-resolution upsampling
Unfair baseline comparison: evaluates against super-resolution methods rather than instruction-based editing methods which are actual task competitors
No user studies for perceptual quality assessment despite claims about visual fidelity; relies solely on automatic metrics inadequate for evaluating editing tasks
Missing computational efficiency analysis despite efficiency motivation; no timing comparisons or computational cost demonstration
Modest quantitative improvements over baselines (HaarPSI differences of 0.01-0.02); not compelling evidence of superiority
Limited evaluation scope: restricted to text-instruction editing; no evaluation on diverse editing tasks (inpainting, object removal) or generalization across diffusion models
Technical clarity issues: hyperparameter τ shows sensitivity but lacks principled guidance; synchronization strategy appears ad-hoc with weak justification
Small dataset of 400 conditioning pairs for comprehensive evaluation of editing method
Appendix G acknowledges suboptimal results due to pretrained model limitations but doesn't adequately address failure modes or generalization concerns

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First to explicitly propose high-resolution image editing as a standalone task, addressing a clear practical need in the field
Technically sound approach: Well-motivated transfer function design and patch-wise synchronization mechanism effectively preserve fine-grained details while avoiding boundary artifacts
Strong experimental results: Consistent improvements across multiple metrics (HaarPSI, M-MSE, M-SSIM, M-PSNR) on both 1K and 2K editing scenarios, with clear superiority over baselines

Comprehensive validation: Thorough ablation studies (Figure 5, Table 2) and qualitative results demonstrating effectiveness across diverse editing scenarios (object replacement, style transfer, background modification)
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-structured paper with effective visualizations; Algorithm 1 provides pseudocode and implementation details facilitate reproduction
Practical significance: Addresses computational constraints of high-resolution editing while preserving semantic content and fine details, with applications across diverse editing tasks
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: Test dataset contains only 400 image-instruction pairs from single source (ChatGPT) with AI-generated images; no evaluation on photographs, real-world images, or user studies validating perceptual quality

Incremental technical novelty: Core components (diffusion trajectories, Tweedie formula, VAE decoding) build on existing work; transfer function is a simple 1×1 convolution lacking principled justification
Incomplete computational analysis: No runtime or memory comparisons provided despite efficiency claims; overhead from synchronization and detail enhancement modules not quantified

Design choice justification: Vertical interpolation weights in Eq. 12 appear empirically ad-hoc; limited ablation on hyperparameter τ (only 3 values); unclear why 1×1 convolutions are optimal for transfer function
Insufficient failure analysis: Section G lacks concrete failure examples; Figure 7 shows boundary artifacts persist; no analysis of which editing operations are problematic or generalization limits

Generalization concerns: Method validated only with Stable Diffusion; unclear transferability to other models; evaluation limited to specific instruction types; reliance on LANG-SAM for masked metrics introduces dependency
Statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; single-run results make stability assessment impossible
Missing implementation details: Transfer function optimization hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, training iterations) not specified; conditioning image selection during training unspecified

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: addresses high-resolution image editing with fine-grained control in an intuitive and useful way
Sound technical approach: proper application of diffusion models, null-text inversion, and learnable transfer functions with mathematically rigorous formulation

Comprehensive experimental validation: includes multiple resolution scenarios, diverse metrics (MSE, SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS, HaarPSI), ablation studies demonstrating component importance, and qualitative results showing detail preservation
Thorough ablation studies: Tables 2-3 and Figures 5, 9 clearly demonstrate the contribution of synchronization strategy and design choices
Good generalization: demonstrated applicability across multiple backbone architectures (Stable Diffusion, FLUX) suggesting broader utility
Clear presentation: well-written with effective figures (especially Figures 2-3) explaining the method pipeline and synchronization strategy
Implementation transparency: provides algorithm pseudocode, detailed hyperparameter specifications, and supplementary material with additional details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (diffusion models, null-text inversion, feature transfer) without fundamental algorithmic innovations; transfer function is simple 1×1 convolution

High computational cost: requires 20.29 GB GPU memory with runtime of 0.74-88.06 sec for 1K and 8.40-36.00 sec for 2K; no direct runtime comparisons with baselines provided; significantly limits practical deployment
Dated baseline comparisons: primary baselines (DIT-SR, DIT4SR) from 2022; recent diffusion-based SR methods and LoRA-based editing approaches mentioned in related work but not empirically compared

Limited evaluation scope: only 100 AI-generated source images; almost exclusively artistic/fantasy imagery with minimal diversity; no evaluation on natural photographs or real-world images; no user studies for perceptual quality validation

Fundamental methodological dependency: method inherits limitations from low-resolution editing; if low-res result is poor, high-res output is constrained; limited discussion of failure modes when low-res editing fails semantically

Insufficient design justification: limited explanation for why 1×1 convolution suffices for transfer function; synchronization weight scheme (Eq. 12) appears empirically derived rather than principled; hyperparameter exploration limited

Artifact persistence: Figure 9 clearly shows boundary artifacts despite synchronization; blended Tweedie helps but doesn't fully eliminate visible seams; some magnified regions show remaining blending artifacts

Reproducibility gaps: no code provided in submission; hyperparameter selection process vague; feature modification term architecture incompletely specified; transfer function training procedure lacks detail

Limited failure case analysis: Section H acknowledges limitations but provides few concrete failure examples; systematic failure mode taxonomy absent; no analysis of when patch-wise editing conflicts with semantic coherence

strengths: Addresses a practical computational problem: editing at low resolution then upscaling reduces the cost of high-resolution image editing
Comprehensive technical presentation with detailed pseudocode, supplementary material, and implementation details that support reproducibility
Quantitative improvements demonstrated over diffusion-based SR baselines (DTI-SR, DFT4SR, PiSA-SR, TSD-SR) on standard metrics across 1K and 2K scenarios
Systematic ablation studies (Tables 2-3) validate design choices including hyperparameter τ, transfer function design, and synchronization strategy
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The core approach (low-res edit → upscale) is conceptually straightforward; transfer functions are simple 1×1 convolutions without principled justification; patch synchronization via blended Tweedie updates is a mechanical combination of existing techniques

Severely limited experimental validation: Small synthetic dataset (100 images); no user studies despite editing being perceptually critical; quantitative metrics alone (masked PSNR/SSIM) insufficient for image editing tasks; no evaluation on diverse editing scenarios (inpainting, semantic manipulation)

Questionable baseline construction: Existing SR methods don't support 2K, so baselines combine low-res editing with Nano Banana upsampler—hybrid approach makes direct comparison problematic and clouds attribution of improvements

Significant computational overhead inadequately addressed: Requires 20.29 GB full precision and 8.40-36.00 GB VRAM; runtime 0.74-88.06 seconds; no efficiency comparisons with baselines undermine claimed advantage over direct high-resolution editing

Method fragility and ad-hoc design: Transfer function design (Eq. 8) lacks theoretical or empirical justification; Figure 9 reveals severe failure modes without synchronization (entire regions become dark/saturated), suggesting brittleness and sensitivity to hyperparameters

Fundamental conceptual gap: Low-resolution editing may not capture fine-grained detail intentions that matter for high-resolution results; no evidence that decomposition preserves editing semantics; potential loss of information about which details matter for the edit

Presentation and clarity issues: Dense mathematical exposition (Eqs. 6-14) difficult to parse; critical details (full precision requirement, Null-text inversion integration) relegated to appendix; informal title overstates claims; some notation inconsistent or unclear

Reproducibility concerns: Method involves numerous design decisions and hyperparameters without comprehensive sensitivity analysis; dataset construction not fully detailed; no mention of code or data release; reliance on multiple pretrained models (SD/FLUX) with unclear integration

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: Addresses practical challenge of high-resolution image editing with intuitive insight that low-resolution editing can guide fine-detail transfer
Technically sound framework: Proper use of diffusion models, null-text inversion for reconstruction, learnable transfer functions, and blended Tweedie-based synchronization for patch consistency

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple strong baselines, two resolution settings, diverse quantitative metrics, extensive qualitative results, ablation studies, and compatibility testing with different backbones (Stable Diffusion, FLUX)
Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements over baselines across metrics and resolutions with compelling visual quality and fine-detail preservation
Good presentation and accessibility: Clear writing, effective illustrative figures, detailed supplementary material with pseudocode and implementation details
Practical generalizability: Method works with different diffusion architectures without requiring high-resolution training data
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Individual components are relatively standard; the contribution primarily engineers a sensible combination of existing techniques (feature modulation, Tweedie estimates) rather than introducing fundamental innovations

Inadequately supported efficiency claims: Runtime varies 100x (0.74-88.06s), memory usage highly variable; paper acknowledges higher overhead while claiming efficiency; no systematic runtime comparisons with baselines

Insufficient hyperparameter analysis: Multiple hyperparameters (τ, patch sizes) with τ ranging 15-35 for optimal performance, but no principled selection strategy or sensitivity analysis provided to practitioners

Patch-based approach limitations: Despite synchronization, method still requires boundary handling; Figure 5(a) shows artifacts remain visible at patch boundaries; unclear if boundary problems are fully resolved

Limited baseline comparisons: Mostly compare against super-resolution methods adapted for editing; few direct comparisons with recent text-driven editing methods; baselines acknowledged as limited to 1K resolution

Narrow evaluation scope: Predominantly AI-generated images with specific prompts; limited real photographic image evaluation; data creation via downsampling may not reflect realistic degradation; no user studies validating edit quality
Inadequate failure mode analysis: Section H is brief (~8 lines); missing systematic discussion of failure cases, problematic edit types, and method applicability boundaries
Overstated novelty claims: Abstract's claim of being 'first to propose high-resolution image editing' is too strong; novelty is in specific LR-to-HR transfer approach, not the capability itself
Unclear reproducibility: No code release plans mentioned; relies on external pretrained models; FLUX adaptations in appendix; full reproducibility depends on model availability
Technical presentation issues: Dense notation in Sections 4.4-4.5; relationship between loss terms and balancing could be clearer; resampling strategy description is convoluted
